label: Title
notes: Open by changing the emotional tone around unboundedness. The lecture is not about sets being too large to control; it is about replacing that largeness by a finite directional certificate. Preview the route from set rays to function horizons and then to optimization consequences.

label: Direction That Never Leaves
notes: Start with the operational picture before the notation. A recession direction is stronger than seeing one faraway point; it asks for an entire half-line from every point of the set. This universal base-point condition is what later makes the cone independent of where the ray starts.

label: Recession Cone Definition
notes: Now attach the notation to the picture. Emphasize that the definition shifts the entire set rather than only a selected point. The cone language follows from positive scaling and convex averaging, while closedness is the condition that lets horizon limits agree cleanly with recession directions.

label: Lineality Space
notes: Lineality is the reversible part of recession. The strip example has both a direction and its negative, so the asymptotic behavior is a genuine line. The pointed cone example has escape, but not in both signs, which is why lineality separates flatness from one-way unboundedness.

label: Boundedness Certificate
notes: This is the first major payoff. For closed convex sets, unboundedness cannot be wild; it produces a nonzero direction at infinity. Explain the compactness idea behind the proof without drowning in details: normalize faraway points, take a limiting direction, and use closed convexity to promote it to a ray.

label: Polyhedron Inequality Test
notes: For polyhedra the recession cone is wonderfully concrete. Substitute x plus t d into every inequality and look at the coefficient of t. If any row has positive drift, a large enough t violates the constraint; if every drift is nonpositive, every forward step remains feasible.

label: Cone Of A Sum Product
notes: Use this slide as a practical calculus, not as a license to forget hypotheses. Products are coordinatewise and intersections retain the directions common to every set. Sums at least contain sums of recession directions; in polyhedral work that is usually the computed rule, while closure-sensitive cases deserve inspection.

label: Recession Of Functions
notes: Move from sets to functions by lifting the graph into its epigraph. The recession function is not an extra definition floating in space; it is the vertical boundary of the epigraph recession cone. The slope formula gives students a calculational version when the function is closed and convex.

label: Epigraph Horizon
notes: The exponential example is the cleanest way to separate flat escape from actual descent. Along negative directions, the graph gets flatter and flatter, so the horizon slope is zero. Along positive directions, growth overwhelms every finite slope, so the recession value is infinite.

label: Level Boundedness
notes: This slide connects horizon slopes to compactness of optimization search regions. The main message is that lower level sets all share the same directions of escape. Once one nonempty level is bounded, the shared cone must be trivial, and boundedness propagates to the rest.

label: Objective Descent Directions
notes: Make the optimization consequence crisp. If the feasible set allows a ray and the objective has negative recession value along that ray, every additional step lowers the objective by a predictable asymptotic amount. For a linear objective, this reduces to the dot product test students already know.

label: No Minimum Failure
notes: Students often compress all unbounded behavior into one failure. Separate the two cases. A negative recession value sends the objective to minus infinity, while a zero recession value can create a finite limiting value that is not attained. The exponential function is the canonical one-dimensional picture.

label: Numerical Ray Finder
notes: This slide makes the theory feel executable. In a polyhedral model, the recession cone comes from homogeneous constraints, and the normalization prevents the zero vector from being the only numerical answer. Then score candidate directions by the objective recession value before trusting a solver output.

label: Rule Ledger
notes: The ledger compresses the section into a usable reference. Each row identifies the object, the recession test, and the consequence. The important teaching move is to keep negative recession, zero recession, lineality, and ordinary unboundedness in separate boxes instead of blending them.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the central inspection habit. The section gives a grammar for behavior at infinity: set rays, reversible lineality, epigraph horizons, shared level-set cones, and optimization escape. Encourage students to classify the direction before trying to interpret an unbounded picture or a solver result.
